the-name.body:
No indigenous ​written attestation ‌survives for ‌this name; ​**Tēzcatlīpōca** is ​a scholarly ​transliteration of ​the reconstructed spoken ​form. Etymologically ‌the name ​means "Smoking ​mirror"[^1].

The ‌ASCII form ​*tezcatlipoca* survives ‌only because the ​early domain-name ‌system could ​not carry ​diacritics; it ​is a ​technological compromise, not ​an ancient ‌spelling. The ​Unicode restoration ‌**Tēzcatlīpōca** recovers ​the vowel ‌length of ​the original directly ‌in the ​address bar. ‌The restoration ​preserves a ​distinctive feature ‌the ASCII ‌form loses — ‌the macrons ​on ē, ​ī, and ‌ō marking ​the long ​vowels — ‌which places the ​name in ​Tier 1.

‌The letter-by-letter ​transformation runs:

‌- **t** ​→ **T** — ​Same
- ​**e** → ​**ē** — ‌Macron: long ‌/eː/
- ​**z** → ‌**z** — Same
​- **c** ​→ **c** ‌— Same
‌- **a** ‌→ **a** ‌— Same
​- **t** → ‌**t** — ​Same
- ​**l** → ​**l** — ‌Same
- ​**i** → ​**ī** — Macron: ​long /iː/
‌- **p** ​→ **p** ​— Same
​- **o** ‌→ **ō** — ​Macron: long ‌/oː/
- ​**c** → ‌**c** — ​Same
- ‌**a** → ‌**a** — Same

​The project ​holds the ​domain **tēzcatlīpōca.com** ​(xn--tzcatlpca-bhb3yro.com) as ‌the canonical ‌home of ​this name[^2].

sources.citation: Florentine Codex (General History of the Things of New Spain), Bernardino de Sahagún; School of American Research, 1577.

overview.body:
**Tēzcatlīpōca** ​(*tezcatlipoca*) — ‌The Smoking ‌Mirror — ​belongs to ​the ​Nahuatl tradition, ​where it ​is catalogued ‌under ​the domain ​"Night, Sorcery, ‌Fate". The ​name means ‌"Smoking ​mirror"[^1].

Tēzcatlīpōca ‌is the ​Aztec night ​given will: ​the ​god of ​the obsidian ‌mirror in ​which ‌all things ​are seen, ‌patron of ​rulers and ‌sorcerers, ​tempter and ‌destroyer of ​his own ​brother ‌Quetzalcōātl. He ‌is not ‌evil — ​he is ​the ‌shadow the ​world requires, ​and the ‌Aztecs honoured ​him ​with their ‌most terrible ​beauty: the ‌year-long ​god made ​flesh.[^2]

PuniCodex ​restores the ​name as ‌**Tēzcatlīpōca** ‌and serves ​its temple ‌at [tēzcatlīpōca.com](https://xn--tzcatlpca-bhb3yro.com). ​The restoration ​preserves ‌a distinctive ‌feature the ‌ASCII form ‌loses ​— the ‌macrons on ​ē, ī, ​and ō ​marking ‌the long ​vowels — ​which places ​the ‌name in ​Tier 1. ​The plain ​ASCII form ‌*tezcatlipoca* ​survives as ‌a modern ​convenience imposed ‌by the ​early ‌domain-name system; ‌the restoration, ​not the ​fallback, ​is the ​form the ‌project defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

original-script.body:
No ​indigenous ‌writing ‌system ​is securely ​attested ​for ​individual ​nahuatl ‌names. ​The ​form shown ‌is ​a ‌modern ​scholarly ‌transliteration.[^1]

​The ​form **Tēzcatlīpōca** ​is ​therefore ​a ‌scholarly ​transliteration ‌rather ​than ‌an attested ​ancient ‌spelling; ​it ‌encodes ​the ​reconstructed ‌sound of ‌the ‌name ​for ​modern ‌use, ​and ​no mark ‌in ​it ​is ‌decorative.

​In ‌Aztec ​writing ​the name ​is ​a ‌rebus: ‌the ​smoking ‌mirror ​itself — ​the ‌obsidian ‌disc ‌with ‌its ​scroll ‌of smoke ​— ​worn ​at ‌his ​temple ​or ​replacing ‌his torn-off ​foot. ​The ​codices ‌draw ​the ‌name ​rather than ‌spell ​it: ‌the ‌smoking ​mirror ​is ​both his ​glyph ‌and ‌his ​body.

sources.citation: Florentine Codex (General History of the Things of New Spain), Bernardino de Sahagún; School of American Research, 1577.

domains.body:
Tēzcatlīpōca ​is the ‌Aztec night ‌given ​will: the ​god of ​the ​obsidian mirror ​in which ‌all ​things are ​seen, patron ‌of ​rulers and ‌sorcerers, tempter ​and ‌destroyer of ​his own ​brother ​Quetzalcōātl. He ​is not ​evil ‌— he ​is the ‌shadow ​the world ‌requires, and ​the ‌Aztecs honoured ​him with ‌their ​most terrible ​beauty: the ‌year-long ‌god made ‌flesh.[^1]

### ​The ​Mirror

Obsidian ‌polished to ​black ​glass: it ‌shows the ​future, ​the hidden, ‌and the ​viewer's true ‌face.

​### The ​Missing Foot

​Torn ​off by ‌the earth-monster ‌Cipactli ​in the ‌creation — ​the ​mirror smokes ‌where the ‌foot ‌was.

### ‌The First ​Sun

‌He was ​the sun ​of ​the first ‌age — ​the ​jaguar sun ​— devoured ‌with ​his world ​when it ​ended.

‌### The ​Ixiptla

At ‌Toxcatl, ​a flawless ‌youth lived ​as ‌the god ‌for a ​year ​— then ​climbed the ​temple ‌steps to ‌die as ​him.

mythology.body:
Tēzcatlīpōca's myths ​are all contest: with ‌the earth-monster, with Quetzalcōātl, ‌with the proud ​— he is the ​force that measures the ​strong by breaking ​them.[^1]

### The Foot ​in the Jaws (The ‌Creation)

To make ​the world, Tēzcatlīpōca and ​Quetzalcōātl descended to the ‌primordial waters where the ​caiman-monster Cipactli floated, ‌all mouths. He offered ​his own foot as ‌bait; the monster ​bit it off, and ​the two gods tore ​Cipactli apart — ​her body becoming the ​earth, her eyes the ‌springs, her mouth ​the cave of creation. ‌Every Aztec king thereafter ​ruled over ground ‌purchased with the god's ​flesh.[^2]

### The Jaguar ‌Sun (The Ages)

​Tēzcatlīpōca was the first ‌sun, Nahui Ocēlōtl, "Four ​Jaguar": his world ​of giants ended when ‌Quetzalcōātl struck him from ‌the sky, and jaguars ‌devoured the people. ​Through the succession of ​suns the two brothers ‌keep unmaking each ​other's worlds — the ​Aztec cosmos is their ‌long quarrel, and ​the present fifth sun ​is only the latest ‌armistice, held together ​by sacrifice.

### The ‌Mirror Trick (The Fall ​of Tula)

Against ​Quetzalcōātl of Tōllān he ​came as a sorcerer: ​he showed the ‌plumed god his true ‌aged face in a ​mirror ("look at ‌your flesh, lord"), tricked ​him into drunkenness and ​incest with his own ‌sister, until the ‌shamed god-king burned his ‌palace and departed eastward ‌on a raft ​of serpents. The Aztecs ‌read the myth as ​history's engine: Tēzcatlīpōca ​destroys every golden age, ​and awaits it at ‌the next shore.

​### Toxcatl (The Festival)

​Each year the Aztecs ​chose a flawless ‌captive youth to be ​the ixiptla — the ​god's living image. ​For a year he ‌walked as Tēzcatlīpōca: taught, ​adorned, honoured with ‌four goddesses as wives. ​At the feast of ‌Toxcatl he climbed the ​temple steps breaking ‌his flutes one by ‌one, and was offered ​at the summit ​— the most beautiful ​death in the Aztec ​year, and the ‌empire's meditation on how ‌divinity wears, and discards, ​the flesh.

sources.citation: Bernardino de Sahagún, Florentine Codex, General History of the Things of New Spain, 1577.
Frances Karttunen, An Analytical Dictionary of Nahuatl, University of Texas Press, 1983.

syncretism.body:
The ​friars ‌made ‌him ​the devil ​— ​Sahagún's ​own ​informants ‌struggle ​with ​the ‌comparison ​— but ‌the ​colonial ‌fusion ​was ​subtler: ​he ​survived ​in ‌Nahua sorcery ​as ‌lord ​of ‌the ​crossroads ‌and ​the ‌dark ​arts, and ​in ‌the ‌Day ‌of ​the ​Dead's ‌night-side. ​Scholars ​compare him ‌with ​the ​Maya ‌Itzamna's ​shadow ‌aspects ​and ​with every ​trickster-sovereign ​from ‌Loki ‌to ​Eshu: ‌the ​god ​who ‌governs by ‌disrupting. ‌Modern ‌Mexican ​art ‌and ​literature ​reclaimed ​him ‌as the ​national ​shadow ​— ‌Paz's ​"other ​Mexico."[^1]

​Within ‌the ​Nahuatl tradition, ‌closely ​related ‌names ​in ‌the ‌corpus ​include ​[[cihuacoatl|Cihuacōātl]], ​[[coatlicue|Cōātlīcue]], [[huitzilopochtli|Huitzilopōchtli]], ​[[itzpapalotl|Itzpapālōtl]], ‌[[mictlantecutli|Mictlāntēcutli]], ‌and ​[[quetzalcoatl|Quetzalcōātl]].

aztec-sources.body: His ​great ‌seat was ‌**Tenochtitlan**: ​south ​of ​the ​Templo Mayor ​stood ‌his ​temple, ​where ‌the Toxcatl ​ixiptla ‌climbed ​to ‌die, ​and the ​excavated ​offerings ​of ​the ‌**Templo Mayor** ​— ‌obsidian, ​jaguar ‌bone, ​the sacrificial ‌knives ​of ‌his ​nights ​— keep ‌his ‌cult ‌in ​the ​archaeology of ‌the ​sacred ​precinct. ‌At ​**Teotihuacan**, the ​Avenue ‌of ​the ‌Dead runs ​through ​the ​city ​his ‌myth makes ‌the ​site ‌of ​the ​sun's creation; ‌at ‌**Tula**, ‌the ‌Toltec ​capital his ‌legend ​overthrew, ​the ​warrior-columns ‌of the ​morning-star ​temple ​mark ‌Quetzalcōātl's ​defeat. His ​mirrors ​— ‌the ​British ‌Museum's John ​Dee ‌mirror ​foremost ‌— ‌are his ​portable ​shrines, ​obsidian ​ground ‌to show ‌the ​hidden.

pronunciation.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation ‌of ​the name ​is ​**/teːs.kat.liː.ˈpoː.ka/** ​— ​Classical ‌Nahuatl.[^1]

​For ​the ‌modern ​speaker, the ‌closest ​approximation ‌is: ​tehs-kaht-lee-POH-kah, ​long ​ō ​on ​the ‌stressed penult.

​Kindred ‌and ​historical ‌forms ​of ‌the ​name:

‌- ​**Nahuatl** — ​Tēzcatlīpōca
‌- ‌**His ‌title** ​— ​Titlacahuan
‌- ​**Owned ​form** — ‌Tēzcatlīpōca

​Tēzcatlīpōca ​is ‌Nahuatl ​for ‌"Smoking ​Mirror": ​tēzcatl (mirror) ​+ ​īpōca ‌(smoking). ‌The ​ē ‌of ​tēzcatl, ​the ‌ī of ‌īpōca, ‌and ‌the ​final ‌ō ​are ​all ​long ‌— the ​macrons ​the ​restoration ‌preserves ​— ​and ​the ‌name ​belongs to ‌the ​god ‌of ​night, ‌sorcery, ‌rulership, ​and ​strife, ​whose obsidian ​mirror ‌shows ‌men ​themselves.
